'''''Carex secta''''' is a [[Cyperaceae|sedge]] from the [[Cyperaceae]] family that is [[endemism|endemic]] to New Zealand.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> It grows in [[wetlands of New Zealand|wetlands]].<ref name="De Lange C.secta">{{cite web |last1=De Lange |first1=P |title=''Carex secta'' fact sheet |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/carex-secta/ |access-date=15 March 2023 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network}}</ref> Its [[Māori language|Māori]] names include '''''pūrei''''', '''''pukio''''' and '''''makura'''''.<ref>Healy, A. J.; Edgar, E. 1980: Flora of New Zealand. Vol. III. Adventive Cyperaceous, Petalous and Spathaceous Monocotyledons. Wellington, Government Printer [http://nzflora.landcareresearch.co.nz/default.aspx?selected=NameDetails&TabNum=0&NameId=FF774E9D-D4AC-4E35-8967-C4DB501D3918]</ref>

==Description==
The genus ''Carex'' is [[Latin]] for sedge and the species ''secta'' means cut or divided, which refers to the divided flower head.<ref name="Champion 2012" /> Sedges are visually similar to [[Poaceae|grasses]] and [[Juncaceae|rushes]] but botanically different. ''Carex secta'' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[monocotyledon]].<ref name="Champion 2012">{{cite book |last1=Champion |first1=P |last2=James |first2=T |last3=Papay |first3=I |last4=Ford |first4=K |title=An illustrated guide to common grasses, sedges and rushes of New Zealand |date=2012 |publisher=New Zealand Plant Protection Society (Inc.)}}</ref>

''Carex secta'' plants can grow up to 3 meters tall.<ref name="Champion 2012" /> The base of the plant can form a clumpy trunk-like structure, measuring up to 1 meter in height and 50 cm in diameter.<ref name="Evert 2013" /> This structure is made up of matted [[rhizome]]s, old culms, which are a structure made of older aerial stems,  old rhizomes and roots.<ref name="Evert 2013">{{cite book |last1=Evert |first1=R |last2=Eichhorn |first2=S |title=Raven biology of plants |date=2013 |publisher=Peter Marshall |edition=8}}</ref> These clumps are usually pale to dark brown in colour.<ref name="Moore 1970">{{cite book |last1=Moore |first1=L |last2=Edgar |first2=E |title=Flora of New Zealand |date=1970 |publisher=Government Printer |location=Wellington}}</ref>

Other identifying features include plant leaves that are triangular in shape.<ref name="Moore 1970" /> The leaves are very narrow, being 1.5–7 mm wide.<ref name="Moore 1970" /> They have a simple leaf margin and are rough to the touch at the edges.<ref name="Moore 1970"/> The leaves are usually longer than or equal in length to the flowers,<ref name="Champion 2012" />  and are pale to light green to yellow green in colour.<ref name="Moore 1970"/> The leaf is channeled (grooved running along the leaf) and very scabrid (having a rough surface).<ref name = "Wetland plants in New Zealand" >{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=P |last2=Brooke |first2=P |title=Wetland plants in New Zealand |date=1998 |publisher=Manaaki Whenua Press}}</ref>

Flower stems, much like the leaves, are drooping, triangular in appearance and abrasive to the touch.<ref name="Moore 1970" /> These drooping culms (stems that hold the fruit) are 0.25-1m tall.<ref name = "Carex secta fact sheet" >{{cite web |last1=de Lange |first1=P. J. |title=Carex secta fact sheet |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/carex-secta/ |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=24 March 2023}}</ref> Flowers are formed on a loosely branching [[panicle]] that measures up to 45 centimetres long.<ref name="Moore 1970" /> The panicle has numerous pale brown spikes that are mostly grouped at the tips of slender branchlets.<ref name="Moore 1970"/> These small [[spikelet]]s at the branchlet ends<ref name="Wetland plants in New Zealand"/> contain both male and female flowers, with the male flowers positioned closer to the tips of each spike and the female flowers sitting further down the panicle, containing two [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]].<ref name="Champion 2012" /> The fruit is a triangular or lens-shaped nut with a short beak that is 2.5–3 mm in length and 1.5 mm wide.<ref name="Champion 2012" /> The utricle (a sac that surrounds the fruit) is 2-5mm,<ref name ="Flora of New Zealand:Volume II" >{{cite book |last1=Edgar |first1=E |last2=Moore |first2=L. B |title=Flora of New Zealand: volume II, indigenous tracheophyte (monocotyledons except graminae) |date=1970 |publisher=Government Printer}}</ref> dark brown with minor winged margins,<ref name="Carex secta fact sheet"/> and contains two stigmas.<ref name="Flora of New Zealand:Volume II"/>

== Range ==
Up to 2000 varieties of ''Carex'' can be found in cold and [[Temperate climate|temperate]] climates as well as on tropical mountain ranges worldwide.<ref name="Champion 2012" /> Within New Zealand, there are 100 species and of those 79 are [[Endemism|endemic]] species. ''Carex secta'' is one of those endemic species.<ref name="Champion 2012" />

''Carex secta'' can tolerate a wide variety of living conditions.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> This species can be found all over New Zealand, in both the [[North Island|North]] and [[South Island]]s as well as [[Stewart Island]].<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> Within this area, ''Carex secta'' can be found from coastal to mountainous areas usually up to 400 meters above sea level.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> ''Carex secta'' can also be found on mainland [[Chatham Island]], although is relatively rare there.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" />

==Habitat==
In New Zealand, sedges are a very common type of swamp plant, and the ''Carex'' family includes the largest sedges.<ref name="Wardle 1991">{{cite book |last1=Wardle |first1=P |title=Vegetation of New Zealand |date=1991 |publisher=The Blackburn Press |edition=first}}</ref> ''Carex secta'' plants thrive in open water environments, which can include swamps, rivers, lakes, ponds, and streams.<ref name="Wardle 1991"/> ''Carex secta''  growth is not inhibited when its roots are saturated,<ref name="Champion 2012" /> and it can tolerate being waterlogged year-round.<ref name="Williams 2005">{{cite web |last1=Williams |first1=K |title=Native plant communities of the Canterbury Plains |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/conservation/native-plants/motukarara-nursery/canterbury-plains-plant-communities-book-full.pdf |website=Department of Conservation |access-date=10 March 2023}}</ref> ''Carex secta'' much prefers water depths between 10 and 30 cm which provide the optimal conditions for growth.<ref name="DoC wetlands protection">{{cite web |title=Wetlands protection guide |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/get-involved/run-a-project/restoration-advice/wetlands-protection/ |website=Department of Conservation |access-date=10 March 2023}}</ref> When naturally dispersed seeds [[Germination|germinate]] in water depths greater than 30 cm, there is an increase in shoot height of the plant but a decrease in the shoot density.<ref name="Sorrell 2012">{{cite journal |last1=Sorrell |first1=B |last2=Tanner |first2=C |last3=Brix |first3=H |title=Regression analysis of growth responses to water depth in three wetland species |journal=AoB Plants |date=2012 |volume=1 |page=Article pls043 |doi=10.1093/aobpla/pls043|pmid=23259044 |pmc=3526336 }}</ref> Due to the ability of ''Carex secta'' to flourish with saturated roots, they are frequently found in [[Riparian zone|riparian planting margins]] across the country.<ref name="DoC wetland planting">{{cite web |title=Wetland and river/stream margin native plants |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/our-work/motukarara-conservation-nursery/canterbury-native-plants-by-area/wetland-and-river-stream-margin-native-plants/ |website=Department of Conservation |access-date=10 March 2023}}</ref> Although ''Carex secta'' typically grows well in wetlands, it can also do well in drier environments.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> ''Carex secta''  are best suited in moist to wet soils.<ref name = "Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lillies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers" >{{cite web |title=Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lilies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers |website=Department of Conservation |publisher=Ecosourced Waikato | url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/get-involved/run-a-project/restoration-advice/native-plant-restoration/ecosource-seeds/collection-and-propagation-guide-grasses/ |access-date=24 March 2023}}</ref> These soils which typically occur in wetlands are generally organic soils<ref name="Hewitt 2021">{{cite book |last1=Hewitt |first1=A, E |last2=Balks |first2=M, R |last3=Lowe |first3=D, J |title=The soils of Aotearoa New Zealand |date=2021 |publisher=Springer Cham}}</ref> or organic [[peat]]y soils.<ref name="Williams 2005" /> Wetlands on the [[West Coast NZ|West Coast]] with a pH between 5.7 and 6.0 provide ideal growth conditions for ''Carex secta''.<ref name="Wardle 1991" /> In these areas, it can succeed in much deeper water, up to 0.6 metres deep and form colonies with ''Carex coriacea''.<ref name="Wardle 1991" />

At the head of the [[Gorge River]] in [[Westland District|South Westland]], which is about 700 metres above sea level, ''Carex secta'' is found above its typical altitude range.<ref name="Wardle 1991" /> It occupies a much shallower habitat in peat soils at this higher elevation.<ref name="Wardle 1991" /> In the [[Copland River|Copland Valley]], also in South Westland, ''Carex secta'' can be found growing at 450 meters above sea level in swamps where [[geothermal activity]] occurs nearby.<ref name="Wardle 1991" />

==Ecology==

===Life cycle/phenology===

''Carex secta'' flowers from late September to early December;<ref name="Carex secta fact sheet"/> this can slightly vary depending on environmental conditions. It will typically fruit between October and March,<ref name="Carex secta fact sheet" /> ripening in the later months<ref name="Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lillies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers" /> before being dispersed. The seeds are dispersed via multiple methods: [[Seed predation|granivory]] (dispersal via seed predators’ consumption),<ref name="Seed dispersal systems in the New Zealand flora">{{cite journal |last1=Thorsen |first1=M |last2=Dickinson |first2=K |last3=Seddon |first3=P |date=2009 |title=Seed dispersal systems in the New Zealand flora |journal=Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=285–309 |doi=10.1016/j.ppees.2009.06.001 |bibcode=2009PPEES..11..285T }}</ref> [[Seed dispersal|anemochory]] (dispersal of seeds via wind),<ref name="Seed dispersal systems in the New Zealand flora" /> and [[Seed dispersal|hydrochory]] (dispersal via water).<ref name="Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lillies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers"/>

Germination of the seeds is dependent on the temperature, taking 3–4 weeks in summer (warmer conditions) and slower in colder conditions.<ref name="Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lillies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers"/> The seeds remain viable in the soil for a long time.<ref name = "Wetland restoration handbook: revegetation" >{{cite book |last1=Clarkson |first1=B |last2=Peters |first2=M |title=Wetland restoration handbook: revegetation |date=2012 |publisher=Landcare Research}}</ref> Because of this, when vegetation is cleared in [[wetland]]s, allowing light to reach ground level, the [[seed]]s will [[Germination|germinate]] in mass.<ref name="Wetland restoration handbook: revegetation"/> Although there have been no specific studies investigating the longevity of ''Carex secta'' seeds, studies conducted on the ''Carex'' genus in the [[Soil seed bank|seed bank]] suggest that some species of ''Carex'' seeds are viable for up to 130 years.<ref name="Schutz 2000">{{cite journal |last1=Schütz |first1=W |title=Ecology of seed dormancy and germination in sedges (Carex) |journal=Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics |date=2000 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=67–89 |doi=10.1078/1433-8319-00005 |bibcode=2000PPEES...3...67S }}</ref>

===Predators, parasites and diseases===

''Carex secta'' has multiple [[Endemism|endemic]] species of [[Lepidoptera]] (moths) and [[Endemism|endemic]] [[Hemiptera]] (true bugs) that feed on it.<ref name = "PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment" >{{Cite web |title=PlantSynz – Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment tool: Database |url=https://plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz/ReportForm.aspx?RecordId=All&Type=P&ReportType=Adv&SortBy=Alpha |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=plant-synz.landcareresearch.co.nz}}</ref> The [[Lepidoptera]] species (in their [[larva]]l (caterpillar) stage) feed on the [[flower]]s/stems/blades of ''Carex secta''.<ref name="PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment"/> These species include ''[[Diplopseustis perieresalis]]'', ''[[Orocrambus angustipennis]]'', ''[[Tmetolophota sulcana]]'', ''[[Sagephora exsanguis]]'', ''[[Megacraspedus]] sp.''.<ref name="PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment"/> The ''[[Hemiptera]]'' species that feed on the [[Leaf|leaves]] and [[seed]]s of the ''Carex secta'' include ''[[Rhopalimorpha]] obscura'' and ''[[Rhopalimorpha]] lineolaris''.<ref name="PlantSynz - Invertebrate herbivore biodiversity assessment"/>

It is likely that [[Moa]] were a herbivore of ''Carex'' species in New Zealand as there has been evidence of ''Carex'', ''[[Phormium]]'', and ''[[Teucridium]]'' seed found in Moa gizzard remains.<ref name="Thorsen 2009">{{cite journal |last1=Thorsen |first1=M |last2=Dickenson |first2=K |last3=Seddon |first3=P |title=Seed dispersal in the New Zealand flora |journal=Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics |date=2009 |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=285–309 |doi=10.1016/j.ppees.2009.06.001 |bibcode=2009PPEES..11..285T }}</ref> Where soil and environmental conditions allow, [[Wilding conifer|wilding pines]] (e.g., ''[[Pinus radiata]]''), [[Cytisus scoparius|Scotch broom]] (''Cytisus scoparius''), [[Willow]] species (''Salix spp.'') and [[blackberry]] (''Rubus fruticosus'') species frequently outcompete native plants, such as ''Carex secta''.<ref name="Landcare 2023">{{cite web |title=Geothermal sidestreams |url=https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/publications/naturally-uncommon-ecosystems/geothermal/geothermal-streamsides/ |website=Landcare Research |access-date=10 March 2023}}</ref> [[willow]]s are a particular threat to the [[habitat]] of ''Carex secta''.<ref name="Wetland plants in New Zealand"/> The spread of [[Invasive species|invasive]] [[willow]]s, with their large canopies, prevents light from reaching the ground level which limits the opportunities for the growth of ''Carex secta'' in what would otherwise be their ideal [[habitat]].

==Similar species==
<!--Note: Only include this if you found out information about this.-->
''Carex sectoides'', which is another species of ''Carex'' endemic to New Zealand, had previously been synonymised with ''Carex secta''.<ref name="DoC antipodes islands" /> This species resides on two of New Zealand's offshore islands, the Chatham Islands and the [[Antipodes Islands|Antipodes]], a cluster of volcanic islands that are 860 km to the southeast of Stewart Island.<ref name="DoC antipodes islands">{{cite web |title=Antipodes Islands |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/get-involved/run-a-project/restoration-advice/wetlands-protection/ |website=Department of Conservation |access-date=23 March 2023}}</ref> The two species were separated in 1970 by Elizabeth Edgar.<ref name="Healy 1980">{{cite book |last1=Healy |first1=A |last2=Edgar |first2=E |title=Flora of New Zealand volume III |date=1980 |publisher=Government Printer}}</ref> ''Carex sectoides'' is far less common than ''Carex secta'', which is widespread on both the North and South Islands as well as Stewart Island.<ref name="Heads 2017">{{cite book |last1=Heads |first1=M |title=Biogeographyof New Zealand's Subantartic Islands and the Chatham Islands |date=2017 |publisher=CRC Press |edition=first}}</ref>

''Carex secta'' has also often been confused with ''Carex virgata'' because ''C. virgata'' can grow raised trunks formed by matted rhizomes and old culms, very similar to the form of  ''Carex secta''.<ref name="DeLange C.virgata" /> The distinguishing characteristics of ''C. virgata'' is that plants can only reach a maximum height of 1.2 meters, which is significantly less than ''C. secta''.<ref name="DeLange C.virgata" /> The ''Carex virgata'' inflorescences are clearly branched and never droop, as the panicle remains rigid and with the basal branchlets often further apart.<ref name="DeLange C.virgata">{{cite web |last1=De Lange |first1=P |title=''Carex virgata'' fact sheet |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/carex-virgata/ |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=14 March 2023}}</ref>

Whilst many native and endemic plants to New Zealand are in various states of decline, as of 2012 ''Carex secta'' is not a threatened plant species.<ref name="De Lange C.secta" /> However, ''Carex tenuiculmis'', a close relative of the ''Carex secta'' that also grows in wetlands, is considered to be more vulnerable.<ref name="Heenan 1997" /> This species can be distinguished from ''Carex secta'' by its red leaves and shorter inflorescence.<ref name="Heenan 1997" /> It is far less abundant than ''Carex secta'' and is considered to be [[conservation status|at risk – declining]].<ref name="Heenan 1997">{{cite journal |last1=Heenan |first1=B |last2=De Lange |first2=P |last3=Murray |first3=B |title=''Carex tenuiculmis'' comb. et. stat. nov. (Cyperaceae), a threatened red-leaved sedge from New Zealand |journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany |date=1997 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=159–165 |doi=10.1080/0028825X.1997.10414152 |bibcode=1997NZJB...35..159H }}</ref>

==Cultural uses==
The leaves of ''Carex secta'' were used as [[Thatching|thatch]] for the roofing of structures.<ref name="Carex secta. Carex spp. Sedges. Pūrei. Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga">{{cite web |date=24 March 2023 |title=Carex secta. Carex spp. Sedges. Pūrei. Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga |url=https://rauropiwhakaoranga.landcareresearch.co.nz/names/99da4e67-bb0f-4069-8aea-02a7ac1053df |website=Manaaki Whenua – Landcare Research}}</ref> [[Māori culture|Māori]] had a [[proverb]] that described ''Carex secta'': "''He pūreirei whakamatuatanga''. A faithful fatherly tuft of rushes.".<ref name="Carex secta. Carex spp. Sedges. Pūrei. Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga" /> The [[proverb]] referred to ''Carex secta'' as a trustworthy and reliable place where you could stop to rest during your journey across the swampy lands.<ref name="Carex secta. Carex spp. Sedges. Pūrei. Ngā Rauropi Whakaoranga" />

Other uses for ''Carex secta'' include ornamental gardening, with it often being included in home gardens and [[landscape architecture]].<ref name="Seed collection and propagation guide for grasses, sedges, lillies, flaxes, epiphytes and climbers"/>

==Sustainability==
''Carex secta'' is a highly important [[species]] in the sustainable management of waterways in New Zealand. It provides multiple benefits to these highly crucial areas that flow across the landscape. One of the key benefits ''Carex secta'' provides is the stabilization of banks alongside streams; its extensive root system holds the soil together which prevents the banks from continuously eroding.<ref name = "How can urban riparian planting chime with residential garden design? An amenity planting trial for urban streamside’s" >{{cite journal |last1=Haines |first1=L |last2=Margetts |first2=J |title=How can urban riparian planting chime with residential garden design? An amenity planting trial for urban streamside's |journal=Royal New Zealand Garden Journal |date=2006 |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=5 |url=https://www.rnzih.org.nz/RNZIH_Journal/Pages_2-5_from_2006_Vol9_No2.pdf}}</ref> Another benefit stemming from the presence of ''Carex secta'' in waterways is the enhancement of water quality due to the reduction in sediment runoff from agriculture practices.<ref name="Wetland restoration handbook: revegetation"/> The drooping form of the leaves of ''Carex secta'' provides an additional benefit of shading over the water, helping to reduce [[eutrophication]] (which can be a major issue in some waterways).

The [[Tussock grass|tussock]] form of ''Carex secta'', raised above the water, provides excellent shelter and nesting sites for ground birds. [[Baillon's crake|''Zapornia pusilla'']] (Baillon's crake) is one of the bird species that nests within the plant.<ref>{{cite web |last1=O'Donnell |first1=C |title=Marsh crake / kotoreke |url=https://nzbirdsonline.org.nz/species/marsh-crake |website=New Zealand Birds Online}}</ref> Another species that has been recorded nesting in ''Carex secta'' is [[Australasian bittern|''Botaurus poiciloptilus'']] (Australasian bittern).<ref name="Wetland restoration handbook: revegetation"/>

''Carex secta'' plants provide refuge for lizards from predators as well as offering them shade.<ref name="Williams 2005" /> Insects have also been found to use ''Carex secta'' as camouflage to avoid predation.<ref name="Williams 2005" />
